25 Years in a Barn: 1974 Dodge Challenger Rocks 340 V8 Muscle and Rare Option in Plain Sight
53 photos
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat
1974 was a year of closure for many of the original pony cars or the Golden Age. The Plymouth Barracuda (the primordial machine that planted the flag in the segment back in 1964), its e-body twin cousin, the Dodge Challenger, the AMC Javelin disappeared altogether. The monikers were discontinued – either forever, or temporary (the Challenger).
Meanwhile, the remaining four (Ford Mustang, Mercury Cougar, Chevrolet Camaro, Pontiac Firebird) went about their separate ways. The FoMoCos transitioned to other platforms (the Cougar grew into a personal luxury, while the Mustang became an alter ego of the compact Pinto), leaving the Camaro and the Firebird as the only two true pony cars.
Mother Mopar ended the ponies without second thought (and later regretted it deeply, toward the end of the decade, when the Firebird and the Camaro scored big in sales – 1979 was the all-time best for both monikers). But that’s history for you – a cruel mistress for the most part, whose lovechildren roam the realms of lore and tale – and sometimes car meets, cruise nights, cars and coffees, and other events centered around nostalgic motoring from bygone years.
Which brings us to this Dodge Challenger finished in factory Golden Fawn (code KY4) over a green vinyl interior, featured recently on the Classic Car ChitChat YouTube channel. Host Kevin Chauhan, the man behind the camera, filmed it last summer in Ontario, and its owner shared the full story of his E-body Mopar icon.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat Although the vlogger calls it a survivor, it isn’t – and it’s easy to see why. This E-body hardtop carries a mechanical upgrade alongside electrical and air-conditioning updates completed by Nick Panaritis of the Nick's Garage YouTube channel in Laval, Quebec.
The owner has a broadcast sheet, and that all-important document helped him trace the car’s origins to august 22, 1973 – so it’s a very early example of that shortened model year, the final of the first generation. Dodge pulled the plug on the Challenger on April 29, 1974 (the Barracuda preceded it in the afterlife on April 1, ten years to the day after it had debuted), and this example is a pole-bearer of that final production run.
The car was assembled with the standard engine – the trusty 318-cube “LA” small-block V8, and the three-speed automatic Torqueflite. The choice of a self-shifting cogbox meant the original buyer could order this car with the regular 2.76 rear end (available only with this engine and transmission combination), or the optional 3.23 (standard issue on the only optional motor, the 360-cubic-inch V8, irrespective of gearbox).
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat Additional factory codes on the tag and build sheet include a V1F full green vinyl roof, C6F6 green vinyl bucket seats, a C16 woodgrain center console, H51 air conditioning, B41 front power disc brakes, J25 3-speed wipers, W21 14-inch Rallye wheels (replaced by now), and the A01 Light Package. Because Chrysler discontinued the 340-cubic-inch V8 at the end of the 1973 model year, no U.S.-market 1974 Challenger ever received a 340 engine from the assembly line.
When new in 1974, this Challenger carried a base price of $3,143 and relied on its factory 318-cubic-inch two-barrel V8 to fire 150 SAE net horsepower at 4,000 rpm and 255 lb-ft of torque at 2,200 rpm. Decades ago, a previous owner replaced that standard 318 unit with a 1968-casting 340-cubic-inch four-barrel V8 (one of the earliest motors of the family, since the famous Mopar small-block debuted in ’68).
It’s a high-winding originally rated at 275 SAE gross horsepower at 5,000 rpm and 340 lb-ft of torque by ChryCo, and around 330 horses by the NHRA officials. That later figure seems so much closer to reality, due to the motor’s quickly-gained reputation for collecting big-block scalps for sport on the street.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat According to Mike, the current caretaker, the Challenger resided in Greensboro, North Carolina, between 1982 and 1984 before moving to Ontario in 1992, where it sat in a barn for over 25 years. The importer sold the coupe to his son, who sold it to a friend in Beamsville, Ontario, owning a rotisserie-restored 1968 Plymouth Road Runner 383. Mike inspected the Challenger on a lift near a Moparfest gathering some eight years ago, and bought it.
Because the car was assembled in August 1973 before 5-mph bumper guards became mandatory, its rechromed bumpers lack rubber bumperettes. All body panels are original and bear the last 8 digits of the VIN on the hood, radiator support, cowl, and trunk lip. Repainted in its one-year-only KY4 Golden Fawn with green pinstripes, the coupe rides on staggered aftermarket Ridler chrome wheels with Cooper Cobra tires and quad exhaust tips.
After a firewall connector burned, Mike shipped the Challenger to Nick Panaritis, who rewired the front harness, installed Classic Auto Air conditioning, detailed the Edelbrock valve covers, bypassed a worn dashboard dimmer bar, and restored the Light Package bulbs. Inside, the green cabin retains its four-pod gauge cluster, three-point seat belts with disconnected starter interlock wires, and a VIN tag reattached with standard rivets during an older dash repair.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat Having previously owned Volkswagen Rabbits and seven Dodge Caravans, Mike definitely car’ed up with this Challenger (which he will leave to his youngest son), the swan song of the emblematic first generation of the legendary nameplate.
The first generation (1970–1974) accounted for 165,437 U.S.-market units (188,611 total with Canadian and export builds). The second generation (1978–1983), a rebadged Mitsubishi Galant Lambda coupe, logged 92,815 U.S. sales, while the third generation (2008–2023) reached roughly 840,000 units.
First-generation U.S. output totaled 76,935 cars in 1970 (83,032 overall), 26,299 in 1971 (29,883 with foreign production), 22,919 in 1972 (26,658), 27,930 in 1973 (32,596 overall), and 11,354 in 1974 (16,437 with the rest of the world included).
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat Across the first generation, Dodge built 25,695 U.S.-specification Challengers equipped with the 340-cubic-inch V8 between 1970 and 1973. In the 1970 inaugural year, 340 output reached 7,196 units, dropped to 2,304 in the following year, then made a comeback in 1972, with 7,760 examples. That jump is explained by Chrysler’s decision to axe the big-blocks from the pony cars, leaving the 225 Slant Six and the 318 as standard powerplants, and the 340 as the alternative.
The same situation was found in1973, when the Challenger moved by 8,435 examples with a 340 cubic-inch motor. In ’74, the small-block was replaced by a 360-cube, to meet the new EPA emission standards.
Although Chrysler's archives did not preserve a full split for all 16,437 Challengers built in 1974, U.S.-shipment records covering 11,354 domestic hardtops list 7,867 cars with the 318 V8 (7,472 TorqueFlite 3-speed automatics and 395 3-speed manuals) and 3,487 cars with the 360 V8 (2,866 TorqueFlite automatics, 488 4-speed manuals, and 133 3-speed manuals).
